extracted.intended_audience: general public (citizens at the time); readers and historians of Abraham Lincoln
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of Abraham Lincoln's private letters and public addresses delivered during his 1860–1861 journey and early administration transition; contains rhetorical posture, policy hints, and statements of political principle. Useful for studying leadership conduct, coalition-building, and public rhetoric in a high-stakes political crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept honors as representative, not personal
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat receptions and compliments as paid to the cause or to the office, not to the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly emphasizes that the receptions are 'not to me personally' but to the Union, Constitution, and the cause represented; advises public figures to deflect personal praise and present themselves as 'an accidental instrument' of a great cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay authoritative policy pronouncements until information is gathered
rubrics_metrics.description: Wait 'until the last moment for a development of the present national difficulties' and 'gain a view of the whole field' before committing to policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln explains his silence: in unprecedented situations it is fitting to obtain full information and light so that when one speaks 'authoritatively' it may be 'as nearly right as possible.' This is guidance for cautious, informed public policy communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise humility and reliance on popular support and providence
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge dependence on the people and on divine aid; present officeholder as servant rather than master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases such as 'I am but an accidental instrument' and appeals to 'that God who has never forsaken' underscore a posture of humility and legitimization through popular will and faith rather than personal boast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule as political legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirm that the majority of the American people should rule; rejection of minority coercion or arbitrary minority control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that if the majority should not rule 'who would be the judge?' and that the alternative (minority control) would be unjust; implies leaders should govern consistent with majority decisions while remaining accountable at elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain composure; avoid inflaming passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Urge citizens and leaders to 'keep cool' and maintain 'self-possession' so artificial crises will dissipate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln characterizes the crisis as 'artificial' and repeatedly counsels temperance and calm, advising against inflammatory rhetoric and turbulent agitation as remedies to political difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and avoid improper 'coercion' or 'invasion'
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully distinguish legitimate governmental acts (holding forts, collecting duties, withholding mails where violated) from invasion/coercion; avoid labeling ordinary federal actions as such without clear hostile intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests asking what users of terms mean and warns that misusing 'coercion'/'invasion' leads to hollow or dangerous positions; use precise definitions before condemning federal actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition-building: regional balance and limited inclusion of opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: When forming a cabinet, seek representation (e.g., a Democrat from New England) for regional/party balance, but limit the number of high-profile opponents (especially from the South) to avoid losing the confidence of one's own supporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln proposes specific candidates and notes the 'danger' of taking more than one man who opposed them in the election; recommends deferring contentious appointments to avoid 'being teased into insanity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint in executive influence over legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer that Congress originate and perfect measures rather than rely on heavy-handed executive influence; avoid a 'very free use' of indirect executive means to control legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States a normative rule: the executive may recommend or veto, but should generally refrain from overusing indirect influence to bias Congress; advises new legislators to 'take an enlarged view' and prepare themselves to contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage and name-use: avoid authorizing others to dispense patronage or use your name
rubrics_metrics.description: Disavow unauthorized claims that one has delegated patronage or allowed use of one's name to influence other elections; maintain a public stance of 'justice to all' without private authorizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln rebukes claims that others dispense patronage in his name or use his name in senatorial contests, insisting such representations are misrepresentations and asking recipients to refrain from using his name in that way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public policy principles: greatest good for greatest number
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor means that 'will give the greatest good to the greatest number' and policies that improve the condition of the working class and the poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endorses homestead-style disposition of government lands to give poor men homes, values equal treatment of immigrants and native-born, and frames policy in utilitarian terms to 'ameliorate the condition of mankind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic policy guidance: tariff to encourage domestic industry and secure revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust imposts to encourage development of domestic industry while providing sufficient revenue and striving for justice across sections and classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reads and endorses the Chicago platform's tariff plank as a guiding principle: promote industrial development, secure liberal wages for working-men, remunerative prices for agriculture, and adequate returns for mechanics and manufacturers; recognizes need to avoid sectional injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concision and prudence in public speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the length of addresses; avoid making commitments in perfunctory appearances; be mindful of personal stamina and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently declines to make long speeches on tour, stating lack of voice or time; frames brief addresses as opportunities to see and be seen rather than to commit to policy, signaling that ceremonial remarks should be concise and noncommittal.
